questions.title: How do you establish coding standards in a full-stack JavaScript team?
questions.quick: I automate whatever can be automated and agree the rest in writing. Prettier settles formatting, ESLint with TypeScript rules catches common problems, commit conventions keep history readable, and a pipeline blocks merges that fail. Judgement topics such as folder structure or error handling go into short decision records the team helps write. I introduce rules gradually, explain the reason for each, and review them regularly so they do not become dogma.
questions.revision: Automate formatting and linting, enforce in CI, agree conventions as short ADRs with the team, introduce gradually and review periodically.
questions.detailed:
Standards work when they are **automatic, agreed and explained**. A typical situation is a team where every pull request carries style arguments; the fix is tooling plus shared decisions.

## Layers of standards

| Layer | Tool or artefact | Enforced by |
|---|---|---|
| Formatting | Prettier | Editor on save, pre-commit hook, CI |
| Code quality | ESLint with TypeScript rules | CI check that blocks merge |
| Commit history | Conventional Commits and commitlint | Commit hook, CI |
| Type safety | TypeScript strict mode | Build |
| Tests | Minimum expectations and examples | Review and CI coverage trend |
| Design choices | Short decision records (ADRs) | Review against the record |

```json
{
  "scripts": {
    "lint": "eslint .",
    "format:check": "prettier --check .",
    "typecheck": "tsc --noEmit"
  }
}
```

## How to introduce them

1. **Start with the pain** the team already feels, not a list of preferences.
2. **Propose, discuss, decide** in a short session; record the result as an ADR.
3. **Automate first**, so review time goes to design, not semicolons.
4. **Apply to new code first**, then fix old code in small, separate commits to keep blame useful.
5. **Review rules quarterly**; remove those that no longer help.

{{diagram:tl-standards}}

## Behaviour matters too

Write a short pull request template, agree review turnaround expectations, and define what a good error handling and logging approach looks like with one worked example.

## Common mistakes

- Debating style manually instead of automating it.
- Introducing a large rule set at once and drowning the team in warnings.
- Imposing rules without reasons, creating resentment.
- Letting exceptions pile up without recording why.

STAR guidance: Situation, review comments were mostly style. Task, free review time and raise consistency. Action, tooling in CI, ADRs, gradual rollout. Result, state your outcome: <your example>.
followUps: How do you handle a senior engineer who rejects a standard?
How do you apply new lint rules to a large legacy codebase?
What belongs in an ADR for a coding convention?

diagrams.title: Standards rollout
diagrams.alt: Pain points are discussed and a rule set is agreed and recorded as a decision record; formatting and linting are automated in editor, hook and pipeline, applied first to new code, and reviewed periodically.

questions.title: How do you break an epic into deliverable slices and manage dependencies?
questions.quick: I slice vertically, so each piece delivers a thin but working path through UI, API and data that a user or tester can see. I start with the smallest end-to-end flow, then add variations. I map dependencies early, on a simple board or diagram, and remove them by agreeing contracts, using mocks or reordering. Risky unknowns go first as short spikes, and every slice has clear acceptance criteria.
questions.revision: Slice vertically into thin end-to-end increments, walking skeleton first, map and reduce dependencies with contracts and mocks, spike risks early.
questions.detailed:
A typical situation is a large epic such as "customer self-service portal" that nobody can estimate or finish. The answer is to slice for **value and learning**, not by technical layer.

## Horizontal versus vertical slicing

| | Horizontal (by layer) | Vertical (end to end) |
|---|---|---|
| Example | "Build all database tables", then "all APIs", then "all screens" | "A user can view one order" through UI, API and data |
| Feedback | Late; nothing demonstrable | Early and frequent |
| Risk | Integration problems found at the end | Found in the first slice |

## Slicing techniques

- **Walking skeleton**: the thinnest path that touches every layer, deployed.
- **Workflow steps**: view, then create, then edit, then delete.
- **Business rules**: one pricing rule first, others later.
- **Data variations**: one user type or product type first.
- **Happy path first**, then error handling and edge cases as separate slices.
- **Spikes**: time-boxed investigations for unknowns, with a defined question and end date.

## Managing dependencies

1. List dependencies: other teams, external APIs, environments, design, data.
2. **Draw them** on a simple board or graph and find the critical path.
3. **Decouple**: agree an API contract and use a mock; use feature flags to merge unfinished work safely.
4. **Reorder** so that blocked work is not started early.
5. Name an **owner and a date** for each external dependency and review in planning.

{{diagram:tl-slices}}

## Good slice checklist

Small enough for a few days, demonstrable, has acceptance criteria, can be tested, and does not leave the system broken.

## Common mistakes

- Slices so large they hide risk.
- Leaving integration to the final sprint.
- Ignoring dependencies until they block.
- Slicing by developer rather than by user value.

STAR guidance: describe a large epic, your slicing approach and what you learned from the first slice. Use <your example> for the outcome.
followUps: How do you decide which slice to deliver first?
How do feature flags help with unfinished slices?
What do you do when an external dependency is late?

diagrams.title: Epic slicing
diagrams.alt: An epic is cut into thin end-to-end slices beginning with a walking skeleton; dependencies are mapped and reduced using contracts and mocks, risky unknowns are explored in spikes, and each slice is delivered and reviewed.

questions.title: How do you work effectively with product owners and QA as a technical lead?
questions.quick: I bring them in early rather than at handover. With the product owner I clarify the problem and outcome, explain technical options and costs in plain language, and agree trade-offs openly. With QA I share design intent, agree acceptance criteria and test approach before coding, and make the system testable through stable environments and test data. We refine stories together so surprises appear before development, not after.
questions.revision: Involve product and QA early: shared story refinement, clear acceptance criteria, options with costs in plain language, testable environments and data.
questions.detailed:
Good delivery needs **three perspectives from the start**: what to build (product), how to build it (engineering) and how we know it works (QA). This is often called the three amigos.

## Working with the product owner

| Do | Why |
|---|---|
| Ask about the outcome, not only the feature | Opens cheaper alternatives |
| Present options with effort, risk and benefit | Lets them make informed trade-offs |
| Translate technical debt into business impact | Gets it prioritised fairly |
| Agree what "done" means before starting | Prevents late disputes |
| Flag risk early and visibly | No surprises at the demo |

## Working with QA

- Include QA in **story refinement**; they spot missing cases early.
- Agree **acceptance criteria** and the **test levels**: unit and integration tests by developers, end-to-end checks by shared effort, exploratory testing by QA.
- Provide **stable test environments and seeded data**, and fast feedback from the pipeline.
- Treat a defect as information about the process, not a person's failure.

```gherkin
Given a customer with an expired card
When they submit payment
Then the order stays pending and a clear message is shown
```

{{diagram:tl-amigos}}

## Handling friction

- **Product wants more than capacity allows**: show the trade-off visually and let them choose what moves.
- **QA finds issues late**: move testing earlier, automate regression, reduce batch size.
- **Developers see QA as a gate**: share quality ownership; developers write tests too.

## Common mistakes

- Handing finished work to QA with no earlier conversation.
- Explaining technology rather than consequences.
- Saying no without offering alternatives.
- Treating the test environment as an afterthought.

STAR guidance: pick a story where early conversation avoided rework. Situation, task, action (three-amigos refinement), result: <your example>.
followUps: How do you explain technical debt to a product owner?
What would you do if QA is a bottleneck?
How do you agree acceptance criteria before development?

diagrams.title: Three amigos
diagrams.alt: The product owner, developer and tester refine each story together; the product owner defines the outcome, the developer proposes options and cost, and the tester defines acceptance and test approach, producing agreed criteria before coding.

questions.title: How do you work with international clients and teams across cultures and time zones?
questions.quick: I make working agreements explicit: overlap hours, response expectations, meeting rhythm and who decides what. I favour clear written updates, short agendas, recorded decisions and visible boards so nobody depends on hallway talk. I avoid idioms, confirm understanding by restating it, and respect local holidays and working styles. Regular demos and honest early risk reports build trust with a client far away.
questions.revision: Explicit working agreements, written-first communication, recorded decisions, overlap hours, restating to confirm, respect for culture, frequent demos.
questions.detailed:
Distance magnifies small misunderstandings. A typical situation is a client in another region who expects daily updates while the team works in a different time zone. The fix is **clarity and rhythm**.

## Working agreements

| Topic | Agree explicitly |
|---|---|
| Overlap | Core hours when everyone is available |
| Response time | For chat, email and urgent issues |
| Meetings | Rhythm, agenda, notes shared afterwards |
| Decisions | Where recorded and who decides |
| Escalation | Route for blockers and incidents |
| Holidays | Shared calendar of local public holidays and leave |

## Communication practice

1. **Write it down**: summaries after meetings, with decisions, owners and dates.
2. **Be precise**: avoid idioms and ambiguous phrases such as "soon" or "quick fix"; use dates and examples.
3. **Check understanding**: ask people to restate in their own words; do not rely on "yes" alone, since agreement has different meanings across cultures.
4. **Use the right channel**: asynchronous for updates, live calls for ambiguity or conflict.
5. **Show progress**: a visible board, short demos each iteration, a weekly status that includes risks.
6. **Rotate inconvenient meeting times** fairly.

{{diagram:tl-distributed}}

## Cultural awareness

Directness, hierarchy and willingness to disagree vary. Learn the client's preferences, invite quiet voices in writing, and avoid assumptions based on stereotypes.

## Common mistakes

- Relying on informal chat for decisions.
- Hiding bad news until a deadline.
- Scheduling every meeting for one side's convenience.
- Assuming silence means agreement.

STAR guidance: describe a communication gap, the working agreement you introduced and how feedback changed: <your example>.
followUps: How do you give bad news to a client early without damaging trust?
How do you run a useful meeting across three time zones?
What do you do when a client's expectations conflict with the team's working hours?

diagrams.title: Distributed collaboration loop
diagrams.alt: Teams agree working rules and overlap hours, communicate asynchronously in writing, hold short live calls for ambiguity, record decisions, and show progress through demos and boards that feed back into the agreement.

questions.title: How do you make a technical decision when information is incomplete?
questions.quick: I first ask how costly and reversible the decision is. If it is easy to reverse, I decide quickly with the best available information. If it is hard to reverse, I invest in reducing the biggest unknowns through a spike or prototype, set a decision deadline, and write down assumptions. Then I choose, record why, and add a trigger to revisit if an assumption proves wrong.
questions.revision: Classify reversibility, time-box learning on the biggest unknowns, state assumptions, decide by a deadline, record it, and set a revisit trigger.
questions.detailed:
Waiting for complete information usually costs more than a reasonable decision. The skill is **matching effort to reversibility**.

## Two kinds of decision

| | Easy to reverse (two-way door) | Hard to reverse (one-way door) |
|---|---|---|
| Examples | A library for a small module, an internal naming choice | Primary database, cloud provider, public API shape |
| Approach | Decide fast, learn from use | Gather evidence, consult, document |
| Who | The team member closest to it | Wider review with accountable owner |

## A practical process

1. **State the decision and the deadline.** Every day of delay has a cost; say what it is.
2. **List what you know, what you assume and what you do not know.**
3. **Rank unknowns by impact** and test the top one or two cheaply: a spike, a prototype, a call to a vendor, a load test.
4. **Prefer options that keep choices open**: abstractions at real seams, small increments, feature flags.
5. **Decide and record** the choice, assumptions and rejected options in a short decision record.
6. **Set a revisit trigger**, for example "if traffic exceeds this level" or "if the vendor changes pricing".

{{diagram:tl-decide}}

## Communicating the decision

Say clearly what is decided, what is still uncertain and how you will learn. Confidence is not the same as certainty; it is better to be transparent than falsely precise.

## Common mistakes

- Analysis paralysis on reversible choices.
- Rushing one-way doors because of pressure.
- Hiding assumptions so they cannot be checked.
- Never revisiting a decision after the facts change.

STAR guidance: use a typical situation such as choosing between two integration approaches with unclear volumes. Describe the spike, the decision and the revisit trigger; for your result use <your example>.
followUps: How do you decide how long a spike should last?
Who should be involved in a one-way-door decision?
How do you recover when an assumption turns out to be wrong?

diagrams.title: Decision under uncertainty
diagrams.alt: Classify the decision by reversibility; reversible decisions are made quickly, while hard-to-reverse ones get a time-boxed spike on the biggest unknowns, then a recorded decision with assumptions and a revisit trigger.

questions.title: How do you handle security and accessibility concerns when delivery pressure is high?
questions.quick: I build them into the normal way of working so they are not extra scope to be cut. Security and accessibility checks sit in the definition of done and in the pipeline. When time is tight, I separate must-fix issues, such as exploitable vulnerabilities or blocked keyboard access, from items that can follow with a dated plan. I make the risk visible to the sponsor and let them make an informed choice.
questions.revision: Build into definition of done and pipeline; triage must-fix versus scheduled; make the risk visible and let the sponsor decide with a dated plan.
questions.detailed:
If security and accessibility are optional extras, they are the first things cut. Make them **part of done**, then triage honestly when time is short.

## Build it into the flow

| Practice | Security | Accessibility |
|---|---|---|
| Definition of done | Input validation, authorisation checked, no secrets in code | Keyboard navigation, labels, contrast, focus order |
| Automated checks | Dependency audit, static analysis, secret scanning | Linting for accessibility, automated page checks |
| Review | Threat questions on new endpoints | Review of new components against a checklist |
| Manual testing | Targeted testing of risky flows | Screen reader and keyboard pass on key journeys |

## Triage when time is short

1. **Must fix before release**: exploitable vulnerabilities, missing authorisation, personal data exposure, journeys unusable by keyboard or screen reader users, legal obligations.
2. **Fix soon with a dated plan**: lower-severity findings with a compensating control.
3. **Backlog**: minor improvements, tracked and visible.

```text
Finding: export endpoint lacks per-user check
Severity: high, exploitable
Decision: block release; fix estimated in one day
```

{{diagram:tl-triage}}

## Communicating the risk

Describe it in business terms: who could be harmed, what the legal or reputational impact is, the cost of fixing now versus later. Offer options, such as reducing scope rather than skipping checks. Record the sponsor's decision.

## Common mistakes

- Leaving checks to a final pre-release phase.
- Treating all findings as equal, which causes either panic or dismissal.
- Accepting risk silently without a record and owner.
- Seeing accessibility as optional polish rather than a legal and usability need in many contexts.

STAR guidance: use "a typical situation is a release date fixed while a review finds an authorisation gap". Describe triage and communication; result: <your example>.
followUps: Which findings would you refuse to ship with?
How do you add accessibility checks to an existing component library?
How do you record an accepted risk?

diagrams.title: Finding triage
diagrams.alt: Each security or accessibility finding is assessed for severity and exploitability; must-fix items block the release, medium items get a dated plan with a compensating control, and minor items go to a visible backlog.

questions.title: How do you guide a team through a production incident, from response to blameless postmortem?
questions.quick: First restore service, then find the cause. I assign clear roles: an incident commander who coordinates, people who investigate, and someone who communicates to stakeholders at regular intervals. We mitigate first, for example by rolling back, and keep a timeline. Afterwards I run a blameless postmortem focused on contributing factors and system improvements, with owned and dated actions that I follow up.
questions.revision: Roles (commander, investigators, communicator), mitigate before root cause, keep a timeline, regular updates, then blameless postmortem with owned actions.
questions.detailed:
A typical situation is an error spike after a release. The leader's job is to **create calm, clarity and speed**, not to debug personally.

## During the incident

| Role | Responsibility |
|---|---|
| Incident commander | Coordinates, decides, keeps the focus on mitigation; does not dive into code |
| Investigators | Examine logs, metrics and recent changes; report findings |
| Communicator | Updates stakeholders and customers on a fixed cadence |
| Scribe | Records timeline, actions and decisions |

1. **Declare** the incident and severity; open one shared channel.
2. **Mitigate first**: rollback, disable a feature flag, scale or fail over. Root cause can wait.
3. **Communicate on a schedule**, even when the update is "no change; investigating".
4. **Keep a timeline** with timestamps for later analysis.
5. **Declare resolved** only when metrics confirm recovery.

{{diagram:tl-incident}}

## Blameless postmortem

Blameless means asking **how the system allowed the error**, not who made it. People who fear blame hide information.

- **Timeline** of events and decisions with the information people had at the time.
- **Contributing factors**: missing alerts, weak tests, unclear runbooks, risky release process.
- **What went well** and where luck helped.
- **Actions**: specific, owned, dated, and prioritised; track them to completion.

```text
Action: add alert on checkout error rate above agreed threshold
Owner: <name>   Due: <date>   Type: detection
```

## Common mistakes

- Everyone investigating, nobody coordinating or communicating.
- Searching for the root cause while customers remain affected.
- Naming and shaming an individual.
- Writing actions that never get owners or deadlines.
- Skipping the postmortem for "small" incidents that repeat.

STAR guidance: describe the roles you set, your communication cadence and the changes after review; for outcomes use <your example>.
followUps: What do you include in a stakeholder update during an incident?
How do you keep a postmortem blameless when a person clearly made a mistake?
How do you make sure postmortem actions actually get done?

diagrams.title: Incident lifecycle
diagrams.alt: An incident is declared with roles assigned, mitigated first, communicated on a schedule and confirmed resolved by metrics; a blameless postmortem then produces owned, dated actions that reduce the chance of recurrence.

questions.title: How do you onboard a new engineer into an existing full-stack team?
questions.quick: I want them shipping something small and real in the first week. Before they start I prepare access, a working local setup guide and a buddy. In week one they run the system locally, read the architecture overview and fix a small, well-chosen issue. After that, scope grows gradually, with regular check-ins on progress and questions. Their fresh eyes also help us find gaps in our documentation.
questions.revision: Prepare access and setup in advance, give a buddy, a small real first task, gradual scope, regular check-ins, and use their feedback to fix docs.
questions.detailed:
Good onboarding shortens time to contribution and signals how the team works. A typical situation is a new joiner waiting days for access and a working environment; preparation prevents that.

## Before day one

- Accounts, repository access, communication channels and tooling ready.
- A **buddy** assigned, separate from the manager.
- A written plan for the first weeks.

## First weeks

| Period | Goal | Activities |
|---|---|---|
| Day 1 to 2 | Working environment | Run the React app, Node API and MongoDB locally with one documented command |
| Week 1 | First contribution | Fix a small, well-defined issue through review and deployment |
| Weeks 2 to 4 | Understanding | Architecture overview, C4 diagrams, key ADRs, pairing on a feature slice |
| Month 2 | Ownership | Own a small feature end to end |

{{diagram:tl-onboard}}

## Practices that help

1. **A good first issue**: small, valuable, low-risk, with clear acceptance criteria.
2. **Pairing** on early tasks, then gradually less.
3. **Documentation walk-through**: ask the newcomer to improve any unclear page they used.
4. **Explain the why**: team conventions with their reasons, not just rules.
5. **Regular one-to-ones** to ask what is confusing and what they need.
6. **Psychological safety**: questions are welcome; no one is expected to know the codebase.

## Adjust for experience

Juniors need more structure and examples; seniors need context, goals and autonomy faster.

## Common mistakes

- No ready environment, so the first days are lost.
- A huge first task with unclear scope.
- Information only in people's heads.
- No feedback loop until the first review at three months.

STAR guidance: describe the onboarding plan you would use and the signs of success, such as a first merged change; for outcomes use <your example>.
followUps: What makes a good first issue?
How would onboarding differ for a senior hire?
How do you measure whether onboarding works?

diagrams.title: Onboarding path
diagrams.alt: Preparation of access and a buddy leads to a working local environment, then a small first contribution, then guided learning of the architecture, and finally ownership of a feature, with check-ins feeding improvements back into preparation.
